narrative.question: When a run ends in ERROR, FLAKY or a surprising FAIL, how do I find out why without paying for more runs?
narrative.viewer_starts: A professional programmer who knows the shell, YAML and regular expressions, and has followed the changelog-entry skill through measuring, grading, judging, pricing, budgets and a regression gate. Knows skill, agent, model, eval file, stimulus, grader, trial, run, workspace, patch (which Vally calls the diff) and the practice folder with its starter; vally eval with -e, --model, --workers and --output-dir; vally lint; the results folder with one folder per trial holding workspace.patch, and results.jsonl with a record per trial; that events.jsonl exists in a trial's folder; the trajectory and its skill_activation event; PASS, FLAKY, FAIL and ERROR, and that ERROR is not a verdict; diff graders such as diff-contains with a pattern, including the (?m) switch that makes a caret match at the start of every line; that every grader must pass and lint's scoring-defaults-applied warning says so; vally grade with --run-dir, which re-grades saved trials for free with diff graders; an LLM judge with a rubric and a judge_model; the timeout under defaults and the max_agent_duration limit; token usage and cost in AIU; --workspace. Has not met the commands field, has not opened events.jsonl, and has no order to look in when a run goes wrong.

arc.viewer_can: name the four questions in order and say which fixes need a new run
say where each question's answer is saved, and tell from a trial's folder how far the trial got
diagnose a broken eval from what its failed run left, fix it, and prove the fix with the cheapest check
match a symptom to where to look and the cheapest proof, and settle validity and completion before believing a verdict

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'When a run goes wrong' in the display serif. Three blocks in a row, no arrows: 'ERROR', 'FLAKY', 'a surprising FAIL', each with a short gloss. They light in turn as the second sentence names them. Under them a lead line: 'Nearly every answer is already on disk'.
narration: Now that our eval files have setup, budgets, judges and several models, more can go wrong that has nothing to do with the skill.
When a run ends in ERROR, or comes out flaky, or fails when nobody expected it to, running it again is tempting.
But a run costs agent runs and minutes, and it usually prints the same error again.
Here, you'll take four broken eval files, find each fault from what the failed run left behind, and prove each fix with the cheapest check.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Four questions, in order'. Four numbered blocks in a row, no arrows: 1 'Is the eval valid?', 2 'Did it complete?', 3 'Why was the result unexpected?', 4 'Does the fix work?'. Each lights as it is asked.
narration: Let's start with the order to look in.
Vally's debugging guide splits the work into four questions, and each has to be answered before the next one means anything.
First: is the eval file valid, so that Vally accepts it at all?
Second: did it complete, so that every trial finished and was graded?
Third: why was the result unexpected, when the trial did finish?
Fourth: does the fix work?
Graders can't be wrong about a trial that didn't finish, and a trial can't finish if the eval file is broken.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Cheapest first'. The same four numbered blocks, each now with where its answer comes from and what it costs: 'vally lint, the run's first lines · free', 'ERROR lines, the trial folder · free', 'evidence, --verbose, the patch · free', 'vally grade, else one new run · cheapest'. The first three light together, then the fourth.
narration: That order is also an order of cost: the first three are answered from what the failed run already printed and saved, for nothing.
Only the fourth may need a new run, and that depends on what the fix changed.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'What did the fix change?'. Two blocks side by side: 'A grader' with 'nothing the agent did changes · grade the saved trials again', and 'The setup, a time limit, the skill' with 'the run itself changes · a new run, often on one model'. Each lights as it is described.
narration: Fixing a grader changes nothing the agent did, so the saved trials can be graded again.
Fixing the setup, or a time limit, changes the run itself, so it needs a new run, and often one model is enough to prove it.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Lint checks the shape'. Two blocks side by side: 'Lint can see' with 'unknown field names · files that don't exist · values of the wrong kind', and 'Lint can't see' with 'what a value means to the program that uses it'. Each lights as it is described.
narration: Those are the questions; here's where each answer is kept, starting with the first.
Vally lint reads an eval file without starting anything, and reports unknown field names, missing files, and values of the wrong kind.
Vally eval runs the same checks before it starts any agent.
What neither can see is what a value means to the program that will use it later.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Commands run before the agent'. Dark code box, left: three lines of YAML, 'agent_environment:', 'commands:', '- echo hello > note.txt'. Callouts on the right: 'after the files are copied, before the agent starts', 'one command per entry, as a string', 'what it creates is starting state: not in the diff'.
narration: One of our four files uses a field we haven't met: commands.
It's a list, under the agent environment, of shell commands that Vally runs in the workspace, after copying the files and before the agent starts.
Each entry is one command, written as a string.
Whatever the commands create is part of the starting state, so it doesn't appear in the trial's diff.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'A colon makes a mapping'. Dark code box, left: two list entries, '- echo note: hello' and, below it, the same line wrapped in quotes. Callouts on the right: 'a mapping: key "echo note", value "hello"' beside the first, 'a string' beside the second. The colon lights, then the first entry, then the quoted one.
narration: There's a trap here, and it's in YAML itself.
Inside a list item, a colon followed by a space turns the line into a key and a value.
So this entry isn't a string: it's a small mapping, with echo note as its key.
Lint accepts it, because a list item is allowed to hold a mapping.
Whatever runs the command then gets a mapping where it expects a string, and says so in its own words.
Putting the whole line in quotes makes it a string again.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'How far did the trial get?'. A three-row table, 'The trial folder holds' and 'What it means': 'metadata.json only' → 'no agent session started: the failure came during setup'; 'events.jsonl, no workspace.patch' → 'the agent started and was stopped'; 'events.jsonl and workspace.patch' → 'the agent finished: look at the grading or the work'. Each row lights as it is described.
narration: Question two is whether each trial completed.
Each trial that didn't is reported as ERROR, with one line of explanation, and the same text is saved in the trial's record in results dot jsonl.
The trial's own folder shows how far it got, by which files exist.
With only metadata dot json, no agent session started, so the failure came during setup.
With a session log, events dot jsonl, but no patch, the agent started and was stopped before it finished.
With both, the agent finished, and anything wrong is in the grading or in the work.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'The end of a stopped session'. Dark code box, left, labelled 'events.jsonl (end), shortened': six event lines ending 'skill.invoked', turn events, 'abort' with reason 'user_initiated', and 'session.usage_checkpoint' with totalNanoAiu. Callouts on the right: 'the skill had loaded', 'stopped from outside the agent', 'what the session had cost'. Each lights in turn.
narration: That session log, events dot jsonl, is the agent's own raw record, one event per line.
It matters here because, when a trial is stopped, it's the one place that shows how far the agent got, and what that cost.
Here's how the log ends when a trial runs out of time.
This line is the skill loading.
This one's type is abort, and its reason says the stop came from outside the agent: here, Vally's time limit.

narration.text: This last one is a usage checkpoint: what the session had cost so far, about three AIU.

narration: So a trial that ends in ERROR isn't free.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Evidence, then the patch'. Dark code box, left: one failing trial's block from a verbose run: the FAIL line, the failing grader with its evidence, the line of turns, tools and tokens, and 'agent output' with the reply. Callouts on the right: 'the grader's evidence', '--verbose adds these', 'the agent's final reply'.
narration: Question three is for a trial that finished with a verdict we didn't expect.
We start with the grader's evidence, the line Vally prints after each failing grader.
Then we go through the trial's patch ourselves, and decide who is wrong: the agent or the grader.
One flag helps here, dash dash verbose: under each failing trial, it adds the number of turns, tool calls and tokens, and the agent's final reply.
Trials stopped mid-session have no final reply, so verbose adds nothing to a timeout.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'A judge call can fail'. Dark code box, left, labelled 'results.jsonl · one grader's record': name users-words, status error, kind llm, passed false, score 0, evidence 'LLM judge failed: …'. Callouts on the right: 'no verdict was reached', 'a placeholder, not a judgement', 'the reason, word for word'.
narration: Graders can also fail to reach a verdict at all.
An LLM judge is a call to another model, and that call can fail; Vally doesn't try it again.
In the trial's record, the grader then has a status of error, which a grader that simply said no doesn't have.
Its score is recorded as zero, although nothing was judged.
The reason is in its evidence, word for word.
In the run's output, the stimulus is reported as ERROR, with a line saying its verdict isn't valid.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'What a re-grade can read'. A four-row table, 'Grader', 'Reads' and 'A re-grade costs': diff graders → the saved diffs → nothing; trajectory graders → the saved trajectories → nothing; a judge → the saved diffs → one judge call per trial; file and script graders → the workspace, which is not kept → ERROR: needs a new run. Rows light as they are described. A note under it: 'anything before or during the agent's session: only a new run shows it'.
narration: Question four is whether the fix works, and vally grade, which re-grades the trials a run saved, is usually the cheapest proof.
Diff graders work from the saved diffs, and trajectory graders from the saved trajectories, so re-grading with them costs nothing.
Re-grading with a judge costs one judge call per trial, and no agent runs.
File and script graders need the workspace, which a saved run doesn't keep, so with them a re-grade ends in ERROR.
Changes to anything before or during the agent's session, such as the setup, the time limit or the skill, only show in a new run.

scenes.chapter: An eval that never starts an agent
scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Four files, one fault each'. A four-row table: the file names merged-list, quick, entry and judged in the first column; the columns 'Fault' and 'Proof of the fix' are empty. The file names light in turn, then the empty 'Proof' column on the question.
narration: That's where the answers are kept; now let's put them to work.
Our starter folder has four eval files, each with one fault.
For each one, we run it once, answer the four questions from what the run left, fix it, and prove the fix with the cheapest check.
Each file's first run goes wrong on purpose.

narration.text: Which of the four fixes would you expect to need a new run?

narration: If you tried it yourself, here's what you'd see.

scenes.on_screen: Terminal in the practice folder; the prompt shows only the folder name. cp -R copies the four broken files in; vally lint on merged-list.eval.yaml prints that the file is valid. The screen is cleared out of sight. Then vally eval on the same file with both models: the end of its output shows two ERROR lines with 'The "command" argument must be of type string. Received an instance of Object', the model summary with 0/1 for each model, the Saved line as ~/src/demo and, last, a warning about a reporter error.

narration.text: First, we copy the four broken files into our practice folder.
Question one: is the first file valid?
And lint says it is.
Question two: does it complete?
This starts one trial on each model, and here we expect both to end in ERROR.
Both did, for the same reason: a command had to be a string, and Vally was handed a mapping.

scenes.on_screen: Terminal, continuing in the practice folder. ls results/lesson-20 shows one folder named with the time of the run; cd into it, its name completed with Tab; ls of haiku's trial folder prints metadata.json and nothing else. Held until it has been read.

narration.text: Let's see how far those trials got, starting with what the run saved.
There's one folder, named with the time of the run, and we change into it.
Inside, each trial has a folder of its own; this one is haiku's.
It holds metadata dot json and nothing else, so no agent session ever started.
So the fault is in the setup, not in the skill.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'YAML read a mapping'. File panel labelled 'broken/merged-list.eval.yaml' showing the whole short file's agent_environment block, with the commands entry '- echo fix: notes add said tittle > merged.txt' marked. A callout beside it: 'key: echo fix'. The entry lights, then the colon after 'fix'.
narration: That brings us to question three: what did the setup do?
Here's the file, with its commands entry.

narration.text: It's the trap we saw, a colon and a space after the word fix, and the same bad value tripped Vally's report writer too.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Quote the whole command'. File panel on the same file after the fix, the commands entry now one quoted string, marked. A callout: 'one string'.
narration: Our fix is to put the whole command in quotes, so it's one string.
That changes the setup, which happens before the agent starts, so proving it takes a run.

scenes.on_screen: Terminal in the practice folder. The same vally eval command with --model claude-haiku-4.5 only; a jump cut; then 'Summary', 'PASS merged-list' and the Saved line.

narration.text: One model is enough to show that the setup works, so this spends one agent run.
About ten seconds later, the stimulus passes.

scenes.chapter: A trial that runs out of time
scenes.on_screen: Terminal in the practice folder. vally eval on broken/quick.eval.yaml with both models and --verbose, over four lines. The end of its output: two ERROR lines, 'Stimulus 'typo-fix' timed out after 5000 ms during turn 1 of 1', the model summary with 0/1 for each model, and the Saved line.

narration.text: Our second file is called quick; it passes lint as well, so we go straight to question two: does it complete?
With verbose added, we'll see whatever detail there is.
This file is set up to run out of time, so we expect ERROR on both models.
Both trials were stopped: the stimulus timed out after five thousand milliseconds.
The verbose flag added nothing, because neither agent had a final reply to show.

scenes.on_screen: Terminal, continuing. cd into this run's folder under results/lesson-20, its name completed with Tab; ls of haiku's trial folder prints events.jsonl and metadata.json, and no workspace.patch.

narration.text: Again we go into the folder this run saved, and look at one trial.
This time there's a session log, events dot jsonl, and no patch: the agent started, and didn't finish.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Stopped, and still paid for'. Dark code box, left, labelled with the trial's events.jsonl: the end of terra's session log from our run: skill.invoked, abort with reason user_initiated, session.usage_checkpoint. Callouts: 'the skill had loaded', 'Vally stopped it', and the cost. Under it a note with each model's cost in AIU.

narration.text: Terra's session log ends the same way: the skill loads, then the abort, then the checkpoint.
What's new is the bill: about three AIU for this trial, and about three quarters of one for the other model's.

narration: That was spent on two trials that produced nothing.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Five seconds is the limit'. File panel labelled 'broken/quick.eval.yaml', its defaults block with 'timeout: 5s' marked. Callouts: 'the hard limit on each trial' and, from our earlier run with budgets, how long this request's two trials took.
narration: Question three: why did they run out of time?
Under defaults, the file sets a timeout of five seconds, and that's the hard limit on each trial.

narration.text: When we ran this same request earlier, with budgets, its two trials took about eight and nine seconds.
So nothing is wrong with the skill or the agent: five seconds just isn't enough for this request.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Three minutes, like the rest'. File panel on the same file after the fix, 'timeout: 3m' marked. A callout: 'the value our other eval files use'.
narration: We change it to three minutes, the value in our other eval files.
This timeout is different from the max agent duration we used before.
That one stops only the agent, and still grades what it had done.
Nothing saved can show a trial finishing, so this fix needs a run too.

scenes.on_screen: Terminal in the practice folder. vally eval on broken/quick.eval.yaml with both models; a jump cut; then the model summary with a tick and 1/1 for each model, and the Saved line.

narration.text: That's two agent runs, one for each model.
This time both trials finish, and both pass.

scenes.chapter: A grader that fails good work
scenes.on_screen: Terminal in the practice folder. vally eval on broken/entry.eval.yaml with both models and --verbose; a jump cut; then the end of the output: under Failures, both models' typo-fix with '✘ adds-an-entry  Pattern /^\+.*notes add/ not found in workspace diff', the model summary with 0/1 for each, and the Saved line.

narration.text: Our third file is called entry; it passes lint too, and we run it with verbose again.
Here we expect both models to fail.
Both failed the same grader, adds an entry: its pattern wasn't found in the workspace diff.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Both agents say they did it'. Two cards side by side, one per model, each a dark box with what --verbose printed for that trial: the line of turns, tools and tokens, and the agent's final reply. Under them, the grader's evidence line in a dark box. Each card lights as it is quoted, then the evidence.
narration: Further up, verbose printed each agent's final reply.

narration.text: Haiku says it added the typo fix to the changelog, under Fixed.
Terra says much the same.

narration: So either both agents are wrong about their own work, or the grader is.

scenes.on_screen: Terminal, continuing. cd into this run's folder, its name completed with Tab; cat of haiku's workspace.patch: an added '### Fixed' heading and an added entry that mentions `notes add`. Held until it has been read.

narration.text: The patch settles question three, so we go into this run's folder and print haiku's.
There's an added Fixed heading, and under it an added entry that mentions notes add.
That's a correct entry, so the grader is the one that's wrong.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'A pattern that can't match'. File panel labelled 'broken/entry.eval.yaml', scrolled to its grader, the pattern '^\+.*notes add' marked. Callouts: 'no (?m) in front' and '^ matches only the start of the patch: diff --git'.
narration: Here's the grader, with its pattern.
It's missing the switch that makes a caret match at the start of every line, so this caret matches only the very start of the patch.
For a diff contains grader, that means the pattern can never match, and the grader can never pass.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Put the switch back'. File panel on the same file after the fix, the pattern '(?m)^\+.*notes add' marked. A callout: 'a fix to a grader: the saved trials can prove it'.
narration: We put the switch back.
This time the fix is in a grader, so the saved trials can prove it.

scenes.on_screen: Terminal in the run's folder; the prompt shows the run's name. vally grade over three lines, with -e pointing at the corrected eval file, --run-dir . and results.jsonl as input. Two blocks, each '✅ typo-fix (1/1 graders passed)' and 'Score: 100.0% | PASSED'.

narration.text: From the run's folder, vally grade applies the corrected grader to the two saved trials, with no agent runs.
It takes the trials from results dot jsonl, and dash dash run dir points at the folder that holds their diffs.
Both blocks now say one of one graders passed.

scenes.on_screen: Terminal in the practice folder, in a smaller font because the lines are long. vally eval on broken/judged.eval.yaml with both models; a jump cut; then the end of the output: two ERROR lines under Failures, each 'users-words · LLM judge failed: Model "claude-sonnet-5-5" is not available in Copilot' followed by the account's list of models, the model summary with 0/1 for each, two lines saying a trial grade is invalid, and the Saved line.

narration.text: Our fourth file passes lint with one warning we know, and it has two graders: a pattern, and a judge.
Here the agents are expected to finish, and the judge call to fail.
Both stimuli are reported as ERROR, and the reason is the judge: its call failed.
Much of what's on screen is the list of models our account does have, and under the summary, each trial's grade is marked as not valid.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Only the judge failed'. Dark code box, left: the top of haiku's block from our run: 'ERROR  cache · 1/2 graders', 'Grading error; verdict is invalid.', '✘ users-words  LLM judge failed: Model "claude-sonnet-5-5" is not available in Copilot.' Callouts: 'the other grader ran, and passed', 'no verdict from the judge', 'not on the account's list'. Below it, a second dark box in large type with the two spellings one above the other, claude-sonnet-5-5 and claude-sonnet-5.5, labelled 'in the eval file' and 'on the account's list'; the hyphen lights, then the dot.
narration: Let's go back to one block, for questions two and three.

narration.text: It says one of two graders, so the pattern grader ran, and it passed.
That means the agents finished, and only the judge failed.
Its evidence gives the reason: the judge model's name isn't on the account's list.
One character differs, just before the last five: the eval file has a hyphen, and the account has a dot.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'One character'. File panel labelled 'broken/judged.eval.yaml' after the fix, the defaults block with 'judge_model: claude-sonnet-5.5' marked, then scrolled to its two graders with the diff-contains grader marked. Callouts: 'a dot, as the account spells it' and 'a diff grader: the run saved the diffs'.
narration: Fixing it takes one character, in the judge model line.
Because this file also has a diff grader, the run saved the diffs, so both trials can be judged again without running an agent.

scenes.on_screen: Terminal in the run's folder, smaller font. vally grade over three lines with --verbose and results.jsonl as input. A warning about scoring, then two blocks for cache, each with the judge's reason, which begins by quoting the new entry, and the pattern grader's evidence: the first '2/2 graders passed' and 'Score: 100.0% | PASSED', the second '1/2 graders passed, 1 failed' and 'Score: 50.0% | FAILED', its reason naming caching.

narration.text: So we re-grade from the run's folder, with verbose, to see the judge's reasons.
That costs two judge calls.
This time the judge reaches a verdict on both trials, and each of its reasons begins by quoting the entry.
The judge passes one, and fails the other, whose entry mentions caching: a real verdict about the work, which is what the fix was for.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Four faults, four proofs'. The table from before, now filled: merged-list · a command read as a mapping · one run, on one model; quick · a five-second timeout · a new run; entry · a pattern without (?m) · vally grade, free; judged · a misnamed judge model · vally grade, two judge calls. The two 'new run' rows light, then the two 'vally grade' rows. A note: the total in agent runs and judge calls.
narration: So here are the four, with what proved each fix.
For the command taken as a mapping, and for the five-second timeout, the fix changed the run itself, so each needed a new run.
For the pattern, and for the judge model's name, the fault was in the grading, so re-grading the saved trials was enough.

narration.text: All four took nine agent runs and two judge calls.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Two looked like verdicts'. Two blocks side by side: 'FAIL' with 'a grader that could not pass', and 'score 0' with 'a judge call that failed'. Each lights as it is described. Under them a lead line: 'valid, then complete, then the verdict'.
narration: So what did those four have in common?
None of them was a fault in the skill.
Two of them looked like results.
Graders that can't pass report a failure that looks just like a real one.
Failed judge calls leave a score of zero.
That's why the order matters: we settle whether the eval is valid, and whether it completed, before believing what any verdict says.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Symptom, place, proof'. A four-row table, 'Symptom', 'Where to look' and 'Cheapest proof of a fix', one row for each fault we met: ERROR in milliseconds; ERROR, timed out; FAIL though the patch looks right; ERROR, grading error. The timeout row lights, then the grading-error row.
narration: It's worth keeping these as a table: the symptom, where to look, and the cheapest proof of a fix.
Two rows deserve a second look.
Timed-out trials still cost money, so running a timeout again without raising the limit pays the same again for the same ERROR.
Judge calls that fail aren't tried again.
So if a judge fails because its service was down for a moment, the trials are still on disk, and re-grading them is the second try.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'What are the four questions?'. One block, 'when a run goes wrong', which opens after the question and a pause into four numbered parts, each lit as it is said: 'Is it valid? · lint, the first lines', 'Did it complete? · ERROR lines, the trial folder', 'Why unexpected? · evidence, --verbose, the patch', 'Does the fix work? · vally grade, or one new run'.
narration: Before you go on: what are the four questions, in order?

narration.text: Is the eval valid: lint and the run's first lines answer that.

narration: Did it complete: the ERROR lines and the trial's folder.
Why was the result unexpected: the grader's evidence, the verbose output, and the patch.
Does the fix work: a re-grade of the saved trials, or one new run when the fix changes the run itself.

scenes.on_screen: 'Next: Keep it working' in the display serif. Below, the hand-off: 'Make it a routine you and a teammate can repeat.' A note: 'Exercises and the full symptom table are on the lesson page · Source: Vally docs, Debugging Evals'.
narration: You can now find out why a run went wrong from what it left behind, and prove a fix with the fewest agent runs.
So we can measure, gate and debug.
What's left is to make it a routine that you and a teammate can repeat.
That's the next lesson.
On the lesson page there are exercises, and a longer table of symptoms to keep.
